picked.t: Lonely Planet's 10 must-visit destinations in Vietnam have most bases covered
picked.body: Lonely Planet describes Vietnam as a destination offering a wide variety of rich experiences. The travel guide recently listed 10 top-rated spots across the country, ranging from cities and tropical islands to beaches and national parks. Hanoi: The ideal gateway for first-time visitors Every journey needs a starting point, and for first-time visitors to Vietnam, the capital city of Hanoi is the perfect place to begin. Beyond its accessible infrastructure, budget-friendly accommodations, world-class cuisine, and rich historical heritage, Hanoi serves as the gateway to iconic destinations such as Ha Long Bay and the renowned trekking routes of the northwest. The city offers an array of attractions and engaging activities. Whatever your itinerary looks like, sampling Hanoi's street food is a must. Insider tip: Grab a draught beer ( bia hoi ) at Ta Hien Street and explore the vibrant food stalls tucked along this famous alley. Photo by My Linh Phong Nha: hub for adventure As the world's largest cave, Son Doong is an awe-inspiring wonder. However, visitor slots are strictly limited and often booked years in advance. Beyond Son Doong, Phong Nha - Ke Bang National Park has countless other caverns waiting to be explored, where thrill-seekers can climb, squeeze through narrow passages, navigate underground rivers by boat, and rappel on ropes. Insider tip: Caves like Tu Lan, Phong Nha, Paradise (Thien Duong), and En offer more accessible price points. On these treks, campers pitch their tents on underground sandbars directly beneath massive sinkholes, illuminated by natural beams of sunlight streaming through the cavern openings. Photo by Jungle Boss Hue: historic destination As the former capital of the Nguyen Dynasty, Vietnam's last royal dynasty, Hue is steeped in imperial history despite suffering heavy damage due to wartime airstrikes. Though many original structures were destroyed, the grand legacy of the ancient capital endures within the Imperial Citadel and the Purple Forbidden City (Tu Cam Thanh). Just beyond the city center lie the royal tombs of Vietnam's former emperors, nestled amidst lush greenery along the Huong river. Another jewel of Hue's heritage is its royal cuisine, widely celebrated as the pinnacle of Vietnamese gastronomy. Don't miss out on trying a steaming bowl of spicy beef noodle soup bun bo Hue or a crispy savory pancake banh khoai . Insider tip: To beat the crowds at the royal tombs, rent a motorbike to explore at your own pace. And be sure to save time for a visit to the renowned Thien Mu pagoda. Photo by Quy Coc Tu Lan Ha Bay and Bai Tu Long Bay: ideal for boat cruises Beyond the world-famous Ha Long Bay, visitors can explore the equally stunning Lan Ha Bay and Bai Tu Long Bay aboard traditional wooden junk boats. You can also kayak through towering limestone karsts, hike forest trails on Cat Ba island, or unwind on the sandy shores of Co To island. The region is also packed with beaches and exceptional seafood restaurants. Insider tip: If you visit Cat Ba island, take time to trek the scenic trails of Cat Ba National Park with a local guide to fully appreciate its untouched nature. Photo by Pham Huy Trung Phu Quoc: haven for relaxation and family getaways Fringed by emerald-green waters and soft, powdery sands, Phu Quoc is the perfect spot to slow down and sip a cocktail as the sun sets. Long popular with both domestic and international travelers, the island offers a wealth of family-friendly attractions, including the VinWonders theme park and Sun World Hon Thom Nature Park. For a change of scenery, visitors can leave the bustling beach crowds behind to explore the dense forests of the island. Insider tip: Numerous airlines operate direct flights to Phu Quoc. Besides, foreign travelers can take advantage of a visa-free policy for stays of up to 30 days. Photo by Sun Group Hoi An: step back in time Once one of Asia’s important trading ports, attracting merchants from far-off lands such as Japan, Spain, and North America, Hoi An is a charming old town characterized by tightly packed shophouses, a centuries-old covered bridge, Chinese assembly halls, Buddhist pagodas, and Confucian temples. History, however, is only part of Hoi An's allure. Many travelers extend their stays for days to attend hands-on cooking classes with local chefs, mastering dishes like "white rose" dumplings ( banh bao banh vac ) and fresh spring rolls. Visitors also flock to the town's famous tailor shops, renowned for high-quality custom clothing at affordable prices. Insider tip: Stay at a homestay in Bho Hoong, a village inhabited by the Co Tu ethnic group. It offers a unique window into local indigenous culture and a peaceful retreat from the bustle of the town. picked.t: Hanoi chicken pho draws crowds despite charging four times average price at $6
picked.body: Situated 100 meters from Hoan Kiem Lake, Huyen Huong Chicken Pho has for years been a go-to destination for both locals and foreigners. In June 2026, the eatery was featured in the Michelin Selected list for the first time. According to the Michelin Guide website, the pho here is highly regarded for its rich broth and generous portions. The restaurant boasts an impressive 4.7 stars out of 5 from nearly 5,300 Google reviews. Owner Thuy Huyen, a third-generation restaurateur, says her family initially sold beef pho before switching to traditional Vietnamese family-style meals in 1986. After 2000, she switched to chicken pho at the current family-owned property, driven by a desire to "preserve the culinary essence of Hanoi." Although she missed the official Michelin Guide ceremony in Hanoi due to a misplaced invitation, she remains confident, asserting that the eatery's quality has "long met Michelin standards." Huyen developed and refined her recipe and cooking techniques on her own over time. Born and raised in Hanoi's old quarter, she describes herself as "meticulous and discerning" when it comes to food. Believing that food must be both "delicious and top-tier," she built her brand around these strict standards. "I use the finest ingredients, put immense care into preparation, and set prices that are high yet fully worthy of the quality." Her place is widely known among Hanoians as "the gourmet chicken pho with prices among the highest in the city." A bowl of pho ranges from VND90,000 to VND160,000, with a fully loaded bowl including chicken liver, gizzard, oviduct, unlaid eggs, blood pudding, pork paste balls, as well as thigh and breast meat. The average price in Hanoi for chicken pho is between VND40,000 and VND60,000. The average price in Hanoi for chicken pho is between VND40,000 and VND60,000. The eatery selects mature chickens raised over longer periods without growth-promoting feed. As a result, the meat remains firm and with a natural chewy texture. Fresh chickens are delivered daily and poached in small batches as orders come in rather than being cooked in bulk beforehand. "It takes more effort, but it guarantees quality, leaving the skin golden and crispy," Huyen explains. The broth is simmered continuously over low heat using pork and chicken bones for over 10 hours and seasoned with ginger, charred onions, fish sauce, sugar, and salt. Every ingredient is carefully used by the owner so as not to overpower the natural taste of the chicken. The eatery has a diverse menu with pho, sticky rice, rice vermicelli, chicken rice, beef pho, and beef rice, but chicken pho remains the undisputed crowd favorite. Diners can also order extra side portions such as boneless chicken or chicken giblets. A group of retired former colleagues, all aged over 70, visited the restaurant for the first time after hearing about it on social media and from their relatives. One of them says: "The portions are generous and the broth is rich and flavorful. While the prices are steep, they align with old quarter standards and are well worth the quality." She adds she wouldn't dine here regularly but would visit occasionally to "treat myself." The restaurant is open throughout the day, has three air-conditioned floors with around 70 covers. Motorbikes can be parked on the sidewalk directly across from the eatery on Bao Khanh Street and cars near St. Joseph's Cathedral. Photos by Hoang Giang
